descriptionChirho: Qal imperative of יָהַב in its primary concrete sense: to give, hand over, or provide something to someone. Used in direct requests and commands for the transfer of physical goods or resources. Attested in patriarchal narratives (Gen 29:21 Rachel demanded of Jacob; Gen 30:1 'give me children'; Gen 47:15-16 Egyptians requesting food from Joseph), tribal allotments (Deut 1:13; Josh 18:4), military contexts (Judg 1:15; 20:7), offerings (1 Sam 14:41; 2 Sam 16:20; Job 6:22), and proverbial wisdom (Prov 30:15). Multilingual evidence uniformly reflects concrete giving: Arabic هاتِ/أعطِ (give/hand over), Korean 주라/주소서 (give/please give), Spanish da/dad (give). Includes feminine imperative הָבִי (Ruth 3:15).

Qal imperative plural of יָהַב in the specialized liturgical sense of ascribing glory, strength, or honor to God. Exclusively used in worship contexts with the formulaic construction הָבוּ לַיהוה ('ascribe to YHWH') followed by כָּבוֹד (glory) or עֹז (strength). Attested in the Song of Moses (Deut 32:3), the psalm of David brought to Asaph (1 Chr 16:28-29, tripled for emphasis), Psalm 29:1-2 (tripled), and Psalm 96:7-8 (tripled). Although etymologically the same verb as 'give,' the liturgical context and fixed collocation with divine attributes create a distinct semantic profile meaning 'acknowledge and declare' rather than 'transfer possession.' Arabic أَعْطُوا/قَدِّمُوا (give/present), Korean 드리라 (offer/render), Spanish dad (give/render).

Qal imperative of יָהַב functioning as an interjection or exhortative particle meaning 'come!' or 'come now!' Used to rally or urge action, having grammaticalized from the concrete sense of 'give' into a discourse particle of exhortation. Attested at the Tower of Babel (Gen 11:3, 4, 7 -- three times with escalating urgency), in Judah's encounter with Tamar (Gen 38:16), and in Pharaoh's speech about the Israelites (Exod 1:10). Multilingual evidence confirms the exhortative function rather than literal giving: Arabic هَلُمَّ (come!), German wohlan/kommen (come now), Korean 자 (come!/let's), Spanish vamos/venid (let's go/come). The parallel development from 'give' to 'come!' is attested in other Semitic languages.

Qal imperative plural of יָהַב in the extended sense of setting or placing something in position. Attested once in 2 Sam 11:15 where David instructs Joab to 'set' Uriah in the front of the fiercest battle. Multilingual evidence distinctly supports the 'place/put' semantics rather than 'give': Arabic ضَعوا (put/place), German setzte (set), French plaça (placed), Korean 두라 (put), Spanish poned (place), Hindi रख (put/place). This usage represents a semantic extension from 'give/hand over' to 'position/deploy,' where the transfer is not of possession but of location, particularly in a military tactical context.
